passage:
Monday: Joseph's hands shook as he played scales for his music teacher, Parveen. "My recital's on Saturday," he whispered. "I'm going to mess up."
Wednesday: Parveen taught him a routine: three slow breaths, shake out his hands, and look at one friendly face. He practised it before each piece.
Saturday: Backstage, his stomach fluttered. He breathed slowly three times, shook his hands and found his mother in the crowd. He played, missed one note, and kept going. Afterwards he said, "I was still nervous, but it didn't stop me."

qa.q: When was Joseph's recital?
qa.a: His recital was on Saturday.

qa.q: What does Joseph saying "I'm going to mess up" show about his feelings?
qa.a: It shows he was anxious and expected to fail.

qa.q: What routine helped Joseph?
qa.a: Three slow breaths, shaking out his hands and looking at one friendly face.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel after the recital?
qa.a: Parveen would likely feel proud that Joseph used the routine and kept going after a mistake. 🎉

grounding: It shows a child recognising nervousness before a recital and using a calming routine over time.

passage: "Zubin, I was so nervous before my board exams that I couldn't eat breakfast. My hands were cold, my mind went blank when I saw the paper. So I made myself a routine. I'd sip water, close my eyes, and breathe slowly, counting. Then I'd read each question twice before writing a word. And I'd start with the easiest question, to warm up. It didn't make the nerves disappear, but they got smaller. Now you try it before your test tomorrow." Varun Chacha squeezed his shoulder.

qa.q: What did Varun do before writing an answer?
qa.a: He read each question twice.

qa.q: What does Varun mean when he says the nerves got smaller?
qa.a: He means he still felt anxious, but the routine helped him feel calmer and more in control.

qa.q: What advice does Varun give Zubin?
qa.a: He suggests sipping water, breathing slowly, reading questions twice and starting with the easiest one.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel hearing that his uncle was nervous too?
qa.a: He might feel less alone and more hopeful about handling his own nerves.

grounding: An elder tells a story of exam nervousness and a calming routine.

passage: The school bus was stuck in traffic on the morning of the maths exam. Ramesh's knee bounced. "We'll be late. I'll forget everything." Shankar, his friend, looked at him. "Remember what Miss said? Slow breath in, slow breath out." Ramesh tried. Once. Twice. His knee slowed. "Now tell me one formula," Shankar said. Ramesh recited the area of a rectangle. By the time they reached school, just in time, he felt steadier. He walked into the exam hall still nervous but calmer.

qa.q: What was stuck in traffic?
qa.a: The school bus was stuck in traffic.

qa.q: What does Ramesh's bouncing knee suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was anxious about being late and forgetting everything.

qa.q: How did Shankar help Ramesh calm down?
qa.a: Shankar reminded him to breathe slowly and asked him to recite a formula.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel helping Ramesh?
qa.a: Shankar may feel glad to be a good friend and a bit calmer himself.

grounding: It shows a child recognising exam nerves and using calming breaths under time pressure.

passage: The colony hall smelled of jasmine and dust. Devika, ten, stood behind the curtain in her dance costume, and her tummy was doing flips. 'My hands are cold,' she whispered. She knew this feeling now. It came before tests too. Manjula maasi had taught her a trick. Devika pressed both feet into the floor, felt the cool tiles and breathed in while counting to four, then out to four. Once, twice, five times. She hummed the first line of the song under her breath. Through the gap in the curtain she saw Maasi in the second row, holding up a thumb. Her heart was still quick, but her hands had stopped shaking when the music began.

qa.q: What did Devika hum under her breath?
qa.a: She hummed the first line of the song.

qa.q: How can you tell Devika recognised her nervousness?
qa.a: She noticed her cold hands and flipping tummy and thought she knew this feeling from before tests.

qa.q: What in Devika's routine could help other children before a performance?
qa.a: Pressing feet into the floor, slow counted breaths and rehearsing the first line are simple steps anyone can use.

qa.q: What might Manjula maasi have felt watching from the second row?
qa.a: She was likely a little nervous for Devika too, and proud to see her use the trick she had taught.

grounding: Shows a child recognising nervousness before a recital and using a calming routine.

passage: 'Bhaiya, I can't sleep.' 'Spelling test?' Varun nodded. 'My hands are all sweaty. What if I forget everything?' Nitin, sixteen, shut his laptop. 'Okay. Where do you feel it?' 'Here.' Varun touched his chest. 'Like a drum.' 'That's your body getting ready. Happens to me before board practicals.' 'Really?' 'Really. Let's do the balloon thing. Breathe into your tummy, slowly. Now let it out like a tyre going flat.' Varun giggled but did it. 'Again.' Three more. 'Now tell me three words you know for sure.' 'Because. Friend. Beautiful.' 'See? They're in there.' Varun lay back. 'The drum is smaller now.' 'Good. Tomorrow, same balloon before you start.'

qa.q: Which three words did Varun say he knew for sure?
qa.a: He said 'because', 'friend' and 'beautiful'.

qa.q: What was Varun worried about before the test?
qa.a: He was afraid he would forget all his spellings, and he felt it as sweaty hands and a drumming chest.

qa.q: Which parts of Nitin's help could Varun reuse on his own?
qa.a: He can notice where he feels the nerves, do slow balloon breaths and remind himself of words he knows.

qa.q: What might change if Nitin had just said 'Stop worrying and sleep'?
qa.a: Varun would likely have felt brushed off, with no way to calm the drum, and might have lain awake longer.

grounding: Shows a child naming exam nervousness and learning a calming breathing routine with a sibling's help.

passage:
The night before my first veena recital, at twelve, I couldn't eat. My fingers felt cold and stiff and my heart kept jumping.
I'm Jeevan. I told Gopika teacher I felt sick. She didn't say “don't be silly.” She said, “That's nervousness. It means you care.” Then she taught me a routine: three slow breaths, shake the hands, play the first line in my head.
On stage, my hands were shaking for the first few notes. I did the breaths again between pieces. By the second raga, I forgot to be scared.
Now before every test I do the same three breaths. They still work.

qa.q: What routine did Gopika teacher teach?
qa.a: Three slow breaths, shake the hands, play the first line in my head.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel the night before the recital?
qa.a: Jeevan felt very nervous, unable to eat, with cold, stiff fingers and a jumping heart.

qa.q: Why did Gopika teacher's words help?
qa.a: She named the feeling as nervousness that shows caring, and gave a simple routine to calm it.

qa.q: How might Gopika teacher feel watching Jeevan play the second raga?
qa.a: She probably feels proud and relieved to see her student calm and playing well 🎶

grounding: A twelve-year-old recognises performance nerves and uses a calming routine.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5. Farhan Qureshi.
Before Friday's maths test, Ankita (ten) came to my desk pale and said her stomach hurt. She had said the same before the last two tests.
I asked her what her body felt like. “Shaky. Like my brain is empty.” I told her that's nervousness, and it's common.
We practised a routine: breathe in for four counts, hold, out for four. Read each question twice before writing. Start with the easiest one.
In the test she did the breathing twice. She finished on time and looked surprised.
Next step: I've taught the routine to the whole class on Monday.

qa.q: What did Ankita say her body felt like?
qa.a: Shaky, like her brain is empty.

qa.q: How was Ankita feeling before the test?
qa.a: She was very nervous and anxious, pale with a stomach ache.

qa.q: What routine helped Ankita, and why?
qa.a: Breathing in and out for four counts, reading questions twice and starting with the easiest, which calmed her and gave her a plan.

qa.q: How might Ankita's classmates benefit when the routine is taught to all?
qa.a: Other nervous children can use it too, and Ankita won't feel she is the only one.

grounding: A teacher helps a ten-year-old recognise test nerves and use a calming routine.

passage:
Sunday night
Tomorrow is the school elocution. I'm speaking on “My Favourite Season.” Two hundred people will be watching.
My legs keep jiggling and I've been to the bathroom four times.
Sudha-didi made me practise in front of the mirror three times. Then she said, “When you walk up, look at the back wall, not the faces. Breathe out slowly before you start.”
I tried it on the stairs. It helped a bit.
I'm still scared. But I know my speech. Didi says being scared means I care.
Going to sleep now. — Divyansh

qa.q: What is the topic of Divyansh's speech?
qa.a: “My Favourite Season.”

qa.q: How is Divyansh feeling the night before the elocution?
qa.a: Divyansh feels scared and nervous, with jiggling legs and many trips to the bathroom.

qa.q: What calming tips did Sudha-didi give?
qa.a: Look at the back wall, not the faces, and breathe out slowly before starting.

qa.q: How might Sudha-didi feel after the elocution if it goes well?
qa.a: She would probably feel proud and happy that her tips helped.

grounding: A young student notices performance nerves and uses an older sister's calming routine.

passage:
The night before the block-level science exam, Vishal couldn't eat. In the courtyard of their house in the kasba, he kept flipping pages.
"My heart is going fast," he told his sister Pooja. "What if I forget everything?"
Pooja sat beside him on the charpai. "That's your body getting ready. Let's slow it down. Breathe in for four, hold, out for four."
They did it five times. Vishal's shoulders came down a little.
"Now close the book. Tell me three things you know about plants."
He told her four.
The next morning, at the exam hall door, Pooja saw him breathe in for four, then walk in.

qa.q: What exam was Vishal worried about?
qa.a: The block-level science exam.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when he said his heart was going fast?
qa.a: Vishal felt anxious and scared that he would forget everything.

qa.q: How can Vishal use what Pooja taught him in other exams?
qa.a: He can do the slow four-count breathing before starting and remind himself of things he already knows.

qa.q: How does Pooja see Vishal's racing heart?
qa.a: Pooja sees it as his body getting ready, not a sign that he will fail.

grounding: In a small town, a child learns a breathing routine to handle exam nerves.

passage:
The music school in Seoul was very quiet before the spring recital. Soo-ah sat backstage, her fingers cold, pressing imaginary keys on her knees.
"My hands are shaking," she whispered to Tomas, who was playing after her.
"Mine too. Watch." Tomas pressed his palms together hard, then let go. "Squeeze, then relax. Five times."
Soo-ah tried it. Her hands felt warmer.
"Now think of the first four notes only," Tomas said. "Not the whole piece."
When her name was called, Soo-ah walked out, sat, took one breath, and played the first four notes. Then the next ones followed.

qa.q: What did Tomas tell Soo-ah to think of?
qa.a: The first four notes only.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling as she pressed imaginary keys on her knees?
qa.a: Soo-ah felt nervous; her hands were cold and shaking before the recital.

qa.q: Which calming steps helped Soo-ah, and why?
qa.a: Squeezing and relaxing her hands warmed and calmed them, and focusing on four notes made the piece feel manageable.

qa.q: How might Tomas feel while sharing his trick?
qa.a: Tomas is nervous too, but helping Soo-ah may make him feel steadier and less alone.

grounding: A child in Korea uses a hand-squeeze routine and small focus to manage recital nerves.

passage:
In the school auditorium, Rukmini waited in the wings for her Tamil poem recitation. Her mouth was dry. She kept whispering the first line.
Shankar, the boy from her class who went on after her, noticed. "You okay?"
"I'll forget," she said.
"Do the thing Ma'am taught us. Feet flat, look at one spot on the back wall, slow breath."
Rukmini pressed her feet into the floor. She found the clock on the back wall. Breathed.
When she walked out, she looked at the clock, not the faces. Her voice wobbled on the first line, then settled.
Afterwards, Shankar gave her a thumbs up.

qa.q: What did Rukmini look at instead of the faces?
qa.a: The clock on the back wall.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when her mouth was dry?
qa.a: Rukmini was very nervous and afraid she would forget her poem.

qa.q: What calming routine helped Rukmini, and how could she use it again?
qa.a: Feet flat, looking at one spot and slow breathing helped; she can use it before any performance or test.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel when Rukmini finishes?
qa.a: Shankar is probably happy for her and glad he reminded her of the routine 👍.

grounding: A child uses a grounding routine to handle nerves before a recitation.

passage:
I'm Chetan, Rehana's classmate. Before our Class 5 recitation, I saw her in the corridor. Her hands were shaking and she kept going to the water cooler.
Then she stood in the corner, closed her eyes, and breathed slowly. I saw her lips move, like she was saying the first line again and again.
When her name was called, she walked up stiffly. Her voice wobbled on the first line, then got steady.
She didn't forget a word. I don't know what she was thinking. But she smiled all through lunch.

qa.q: Where did Rehana keep going before the recitation?
qa.a: To the water cooler.

qa.q: How was Rehana feeling before her turn?
qa.a: She felt nervous; her hands were shaking.

qa.q: What calming routine did Rehana use?
qa.a: She breathed slowly with her eyes closed and repeated the first line.

qa.q: How does Chetan see Rehana's recitation?
qa.a: Chetan seems impressed, noticing her voice steadied, though unsure what she was thinking.

grounding: A classmate observes a child using a calming routine before a recitation.

passage:
Winter exam week, Monday: Madhav, ten, woke with a tummy ache before his first exam. He cried and said he'd forgotten everything.
Wednesday: His uncle Santosh taught him "five things": name five things you see, four you hear, three you touch. Madhav practised on the bus.
Next Monday: Before the science exam, Madhav felt his tummy knot. He did the five things quietly. His breathing slowed. He wrote his name and began.

qa.q: What routine did Santosh teach?
qa.a: "Five things": name five things you see, four you hear, three you touch.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel before his first exam?
qa.a: He felt nervous and scared, with a tummy ache, crying.

qa.q: How did the routine help Madhav?
qa.a: It calmed his breathing and focus so he could start the exam.

qa.q: How might Santosh feel hearing it helped?
qa.a: Santosh likely feels proud and relieved.

passage:
Yamini, you're shaking before your dance show? Come, sit. Let me tell you about me when I was nine, at the spring festival.
I, Dolma, had to sing in front of the whole monastery school. My legs felt like water. I thought I'd faint.
My grandmother held my hands and said, "Breathe like you're smelling flowers, then blow out a candle." I did it five times.
My voice shook at first. Then it got strong. Everyone clapped.
Before every stage since, I do the flowers and candle. So, Yamini, smell the flowers.

qa.q: What did the grandmother tell Dolma to breathe like?
qa.a: Smelling flowers, then blowing out a candle.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel before singing?
qa.a: Dolma felt very nervous; the legs felt like water.

qa.q: What was the key choice in Dolma's story?
qa.a: Using the grandmother's breathing trick, which Dolma kept using for every stage.

qa.q: How might the grandmother have felt when Dolma sang?
qa.a: Dolma's grandmother likely felt proud and happy.

grounding: An elder recalls learning a breathing routine for stage nerves as a child.

passage:
The winter fog was so thick the school bus crawled, and Yusuf's music recital started in twenty minutes. He had the flute solo.
His hands were cold and shaking. His heart was thumping. "What if I forget the middle part?" he whispered.
His friend Tushar, sitting beside him, said, "Do your thing. The counting thing."
Yusuf closed his eyes. Breathe in for four, hold for four, out for four. He pressed his fingers along the flute in his lap, playing the tune silently from start to end.
The bus arrived with five minutes to spare. On stage, his first note wobbled. He took one slow breath and kept going.
Afterwards, Tushar punched his arm gently. "The middle part was the best bit."

qa.q: How many minutes did the bus have to spare when it arrived?
qa.a: The bus arrived with five minutes to spare.

qa.q: What might Yusuf be worried about on the bus?
qa.a: He was nervous and afraid he would forget the middle part of his flute solo.

qa.q: What calming routine could Yusuf use again before a performance?
qa.a: He could repeat the breathing for four counts and play the tune silently with his fingers, which steadied him even when the bus was late.

qa.q: How does Tushar help Yusuf feel more confident?
qa.a: Tushar reminds him of his calming routine and cheers him after, so Yusuf feels supported and less alone with his nerves.

grounding: Shows a child noticing performance nerves and using a calming routine despite a late, foggy bus ride.
